Minimal pairs contrasting in the placement of stress have not been found for three major word-classes, Nouns, Verbs, and Pronouns. H. Hymes (Harvard), and printed page numbers 238 and 241, so the extract is the real article, IJAL 22(4). Every piece of the stitched quote is present verbatim at the stated locators: p. 238 §0 'There is one phoneme of stress in Wishram Chinook, as apparently in all other Chinookan dialects.[fn 1] Minimal pairs contrasting in the placement of stress have not been found for three major word-classes, Nouns, Verbs, and Pronouns.'; p. 238 'Thus, while no one general rule can be given, the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One culminative primary stress per word; its position is not given by a single phonological rule but by morphology: polysyllabic stems are stressed on the first syllable of the stem, while non-syllabic and monosyllabic stems throw the stress onto the immediately preceding prefix syllable (directive u-, syllabic adverbial or object prefix); certain prefixes (possessive a-, x-t- reflexive+directive) attract stress and certain suffixes (-x, -lal, -nan, -mama, -lx, -ptk, -wulx, distributive plural -max, local-relational -ba/-yamt) draw it rightward; pronouns and particles are stressed on the first syllable, reduplicated particles on the second element. These regularities are overridden by an alternating (iambic) sentence rhythm and by rhetorical accent, and the authors state the rules are 'not mechanically operative' and stress is 'partly unpredictable' (p. 241).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Typically a word has one and only one phonemic stress, but predictable secondary stress occurs on alternate syllables preceding and following that syllable with primary, phonemic stress. This alternating, iambic pattern tends to prevail in sequences of words also.' (p. 238)
new_statements.exceptions: A handful of particle minimal pairs (bama 'in order that' vs bamá 'since'; Wasco k'wálalak 'drunk' vs k'walalák 'crazy'; kwádau 'and' vs kwadáu 'now, first'); rhythmic alternation of the same word (tgwiwálal/tgwíwalal, gayúya/gáyuya) and haplology aga gayúya > agayúya when three unstressed syllables would intervene; rhetorical word-final accent with vowel lengthening (itgwálilx vs itgwalé·lx); a few verbs always stem-stressed (galix-k'wá); aga and future alma normally unstressed; Wishram lacks the 'inorganic schwa' that bears accent in Shoalwater and Kathlamet.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress but explicitly conditioned by sentence rhythm: in two-word phrases the first word takes the stronger stress and the second may be reduced or lost; data from Dyk's 1930-31 Wishram fieldwork (informant Philip Kahclamat) plus Sapir 1905 texts and Hymes' 1951/1954 Wasco fieldwork; running text rather than citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Dyk & Hymes 1956 describe Wishram (Dyk's 1930-31 fieldwork, informant Philip Kahclamat, plus Sapir's 1905 Wishram texts) with comparative Wasco notes from Hymes' 1951/1954 fieldwork; Wishram and Wasco are the two named Kiksht dialects that Glottolog lists under wasc1239 (alternative names Kiksht, Wasco, Wishram; no separate dialect glottocodes). Kathlamet (kath1253) and Shoalwater Lower Chinook are only contrasted (they have accent-bearing inorganic schwa, which Wishram lacks). The 1956 statement covers the Wishram-Wasco variety, not Clackamas or Cascades.

Minimal pairs contrasting in the placement of stress have not been found for three major word-classes, Nouns, Verbs, and Pronouns. [...] Thus, while no one general rule can be given, the patterns that occur seem to involve but three kinds of factors; these are sentence rhythm, rhetorical uses of stress, and the effect of certain morphemic elements. sources.note: Whole article on stress: one phoneme of stress, one primary stress per word with predictable alternating secondary stress; placement governed by (1) sentence rhythm, (2) rhetorical accent, (3) morphemic elements - polysyllabic stems stressed on first stem syllable, non-/monosyllabic stems put stress on the preceding prefix syllable, possessive a-, pronoun/particle first syllables accented, suffixes -x -lal -max etc. draw accent rightward; authors conclude the rules are 'not mechanically operative' and stress is 'partly unpredictable', with a handful of particle minimal pairs (bama/bamá).
